blocks.text: Poverty is a state or condition in which an individual lacks the financial resources and essentials for a basic standard of living. It can have diverse environmental, legal, social, economic, and political causes and effects.
1. Absolute Poverty: A condition where individuals lack basic necessities like food, clean water, shelter, clothing, and healthcare, and education.
2. Relative Poverty: A condition where individuals have significantly lower income or resources compared to the average income level of their society.

3. Subjective Poverty: A condition based on personal perceptions of economic well-being, where individuals feel poor, despite their income level influenced by societal comparisons, personal expectations, and psychological factors.
Poverty Estimation Poverty Gap Index: It is used to measure the depth of poverty by accounting for the extent to which individuals fall below the poverty line.
The World Poverty Clock: It is managed by World Data Lab, provides real-time estimates of global poverty.

Pre-Independence Estimation
Dadabhai Naoroji through his book, "Poverty and Unbritish Rule in India" made the earliest estimation of poverty line (%16 to %35 per capita per year).
He was the first person to give estimation of National Income of India.
1. National Planning Committee (1938) elt was set up by Subash Chandra Bose under the chairmanship of JL Nehru.

The National Planning Committee (NPC) of 1938 estimated the poverty line at %15 to %20 per capita per month. eThis estimate was based on a minimum standard of living which implicitly included nutritional requirements.
2. The Bombay Plan (1944)
It was a set of proposals by influential business leaders in Bombay for the development of India.
Poverty line was suggested as: 75 per capita per year.
Post-Independence Estimation 1. VM Dandekar and N Rath (1971)
It was the first systematic assessment of poverty in India, based on National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data.
It was an Expenditure based Poverty line estimation. elt is adequate to provide 2250 calories per day in rural and urban areas.
2. Alagh Committee (1979) eThe Planning Committee constituted Alagh Committee under the chairmanship of YK Alagh.
He constructed a poverty line for rural and urban areas on the basis of nutritional requirements and related consumption expenditure.
Rural: 2400 calories > Rs 49.09 per month
Urban: 2100 calories > Rs 56.64 per month 3. Lakadawala Committee (1993)
This committee defined the poverty line on the basis of household per capita consumption expenditure.
The committee used Consumer Price Index-Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) and CPI-AL (Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Laborers) for estimation of the poverty line.
It made few suggestions:
Consumption expenditure should be calculated based on calorie consumption as earlier.
State specific poverty lines should be constructed.

A current account deficit is when a country imports more than it exports.
It includes the balance of trade, net income from abroad, foreign aid, and net current transfers.
A twin deficit occurs when a country has both a current account deficit and a fiscal deficit.
Balance of Payment Crisis (1991)

Balance of Payment (BoP) Crisis is also called currency crisis. It occurs when a nation is unable to pay for essential imports or repay its foreign debts. eIndia faced BOP in 1991 (then PM: PV Narasimha Rao and then Finance Minister: Manmohan Singh). NOSTRO and VOSTRO eA Nostro ("our") account refers to a bank account that a domestic bank holds in a foreign bank in foreign currency >"Our account/money in your bank". It is used for international transactions and trade.

A VOSTRO ("your") account refers to a bank account that a foreign bank holds in a domestic bank in the domestic currency > "Your account/money in our bank". It allows foreign banks to conduct transactions in the domestic market.
FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1973)

It was introduced with the intent to facilitate and simplify the foreign exchange system in India. This act was later abolished and replaced by FEMA since its rigid regulations were hindering India's economic growth.
Under FERA it was treated as Criminal Offence.
FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999)

FEMA focuses on enhancing India's foreign exchange reserves and emphasises the promotion of foreign trade and payments. e[t decriminalised the criminal offence violation into civil offence making it more user friendly.
Certain Terms to Understand
Depreciation: A decrease in the value of the domestic currency due to market forces (supply and demand in the forex market). Exporters will benefit in case of depreciation.
Appreciation: An increase in the value of the domestic currency due to market forces. This happens when the demand for the domestic currency rises.
"Both Depreciation and Appreciation occurs due to Floating Exchange Rate system (price of country's currency is determined by the market based on supply and demand).
Devaluation: A government-induced depreciation of the domestic currency under a fixed exchange rate system.
Devaluation of currency will be more beneficial if prices of exports rise proportionately.
Revaluation: A government-induced appreciation of the domestic currency under a fixed exchange rate system.

Current Account Convertibility:
Freedom to convert rupee for trade transactions (imports, exports, remittances, travel, etc.)
India adopted full current account convertibility in 1994 under IMF Article VIII.
Capital Account Convertibility:
Freedom to convert rupee for capital transactions such as foreign investment, loans, and purchase of assets abroad.
In India it is partially convertible and regulated by the Reserve Bank of India.

It was constituted in 1997, reviewed again in 2006, constituted by the Reserve Bank of India under the chairmanship of S. S. Exchange Rate System in India Evolution of Exchange Rate Regime in India
1928-1948: Indian Rupee pegged to British Pound Sterling.
Post-1948 (IMF System): Rupee pegged to US Dollar under Fixed Exchange Rate System (value fixed by government).
1975: India delinked Rupee from Pound Sterling.
1992: Introduction of LERMS (Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System) — Dual exchange rate system (partly government controlled and partly market determined).
1993: India adopted a Market Determined / Floating Exchange Rate System where demand and supply decide the value of Rupee.
NEER (Nominal Effective Exchange Rate):
Weighted average of the domestic currency against a basket of foreign currencies based on trade weights; does not adjust for inflation.
REER (Real Effective Exchange Rate):
NEER adjusted for inflation (price differential); shows the real external value or competitiveness of the currency.
Hard Currency: A stable and widely accepted currency with strong value in international trade (e.g., USD, Euro).
Soft Currency: A weak and unstable currency that is not widely accepted globally.
Hot Currency: Currency that moves quickly between countries for short-term profit due to interest rate or exchange rate changes.
Heated Currency: Currency under heavy demand or speculation in the foreign exchange market.
Cheap Currency: A currency whose value has depreciated (low exchange value) compared to others.
Dear Currency: A currency whose value has appreciated (high exchange value) compared to others.
Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)

Base Erosion: Establishing shell companies in different jurisdiction to break audit trail and separate the money from source.This involves reducing the level of taxable profits within a specific high-tax jurisdiction.

Profit Shifting: This is the actual movement of those "eroded" profits from a high-tax jurisdiction to a low or no- tax jurisdiction, such as the Cayman Islands or Bahamas, where there is little to no actual economic activity.
Round Tripping:

Round tripping refers to the process where domestic black money is sent abroad and then brought back into the country as foreign investment (FDI) through shell companies or tax havens to make it appear legitimate.

A shell company is a corporate entity that exists only on paper with little or no real business operations, often used to hold assets, route funds, or conceal the real ownership of money.

Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) elt is a provision under Section 115JB of the Income Tax Act, 1961, ensuring companies that claim high exemptions/ incentives still pay a minimum tax. It applies when the normal tax liability is less than 15% of their book profit (plus surcharge/cess).

Concept: Companies sometimes reduce taxable income using incentives (like depreciation, SEZ benefits, etc.). MAT ensures they pay at least a minimum tax based on "book profit" (profit as per financial statements), not just taxable income.
Applicability: Applies to all domestic and foreign companies.
Calculation: Book profit is calculated according to the Companies Act 2013.
Purpose: To prevent "zero-tax" companies from avoiding tax, even if they are profitable. gan
